title: Germany's antitrust watchdog launches market probe into Google Maps in cars
summary: Germany's antitrust watchdog launches market probe into Google Maps in cars
detailed: Germany's federal competition authority, the Bundeskartellamt, opened a market consultation into Google's automotive mapping services on November 9, 2026.
The probe examines the Google Automotive SDK to determine whether Google unfairly restricts carmakers from buying navigation and map features individually rather than as a bundled package.
The antitrust watchdog is investigating potential impacts on rival map providers and whether the setup limits interoperability with competitor services.
The SDK allows automotive manufacturers to integrate Google's traffic routing and POI search into vehicle infotainment systems, with early adopters including Rivian and XPeng.
sentences: The Bundeskartellamt, Germany's federal competition authority, opened a market consultation on November 9, 2026 into the mapping services Google sells to carmakers.
It wants to know whether the Google Automotive SDK, the navigation package built for infotainment systems, keeps manufacturers from mixing Google's services with those of its competitors.
The Bundeskartellamt is based in Bonn and, for the big digital groups, it has dedicated rules at its disposal, section 19a of the German Act against Restraints of Competition (GWB).
Those rules let the authority ban certain practices in two steps for companies of paramount significance across markets.
On that basis it had opened or closed, up to 2025, proceedings against Amazon, Apple, Meta and Microsoft.
Now it is Google's turn again.
Infotainment is the computer hiding behind the car's central screen, running navigation and apps.
Google supplies it through several offerings.
The best known is Google Automotive Services (Maps, Play Store and Assistant, the so-called Google built into the car).
The newest is the Google Automotive SDK, a software development kit (SDK) that lets a carmaker build its own navigator on top of Mountain View's technology.
In its press release of November 9, the authority moves on two fronts.
The first concerns the SDK itself, recently launched and aimed at manufacturers.
The package includes map data, search for points of interest (POIs, for example fuel stations and charging points), navigation functions and real-time traffic information.
The Kartellamt suspects that Google offers these services only together, leaving customers no way to buy them one by one and pair them with those of other suppliers.
A hypothetical example shows what is at stake.

A carmaker might want Google's place search, where the authority itself recognized a unique position in 2025 (the result of the group's services being widespread among users), but the traffic data of another supplier.
If the package can only be bought whole, that combination is off the table.
The second front concerns the Google Maps Platform, the line of mapping services Google licenses to logistics and delivery companies so they can build them into their own applications.
The authority has to establish whether, for a carmaker, this offering is an equivalent alternative to buying the individual SDK components.
It also has to work out whether the way the Maps Platform is set up in the auto sector makes interoperability harder, meaning the ability of Google's services to work alongside those of rivals.

“What matters for competition is that vehicle manufacturers can freely choose between different providers and combine their map services according to their own needs,” said Andreas Mundt, president of the Bundeskartellamt, in the release.

“If these options are restricted, other map providers can suffer and, in the end, so can the offering for drivers.”
The consultation is aimed at carmakers and other map providers.
Anyone who has not been contacted can write to info@bundeskartellamt.bund.de.
Mundt also warns that “numerous, in part highly technical questions” remain open.
The consultation exists precisely to gather the evidence needed to judge whether the changes Google has announced are enough to dispel the doubts.
An SDK is a toolbox, a set of libraries and tools a company makes available so others can build a product on top of its technology.
In the car, the manufacturer keeps the interface customers already know, while Google works underneath with traffic-aware routing, place search and energy and trip estimates for electric vehicles.
According to Electrek , the first to use it was the American Rivian , in July 2025.
A year later China's XPeng fitted the SDK to the L03, unveiled in Munich, in place of the navigation system on its overseas markets (in China the company keeps using its own maps).
XPeng ties the choice to assisted driving as well.
Outside China, its NGP system needs data and navigation maneuvers that manufacturers struggle to cover on their own across dozens of countries.
On those same cars we had already seen Google Play arrive from 2027, with no smartphone needed .
Google told heise that the SDK is in use at selected manufacturers outside Europe and that it is now offering it to European ones as well.
Judging by those words, the product is at an early stage in Europe and the probe arrives before it spreads.
For its part, Google responded on two levels.

It told the authority it is in continuous dialogue and announced that it will reorganize and standardize the Google Maps Platform offering for the auto sector under the name Geo Cloud Automotive Program.

It explained to heise that under the new program manufacturers will be able to choose modularly between the Automotive SDK and equivalent individual components, with interoperability toward third-party services guaranteed and with protection for user security and data.
Google itself says that, after last year's agreements with the authority, it moved the developer offering from the Maps Platform interface to the more integrated Automotive SDK.
It adds that it never intended to shut down or scale back existing automotive services and calls the consultation a normal step in the procedure.
The Kartellamt's logic is straightforward.
If the individual components exist and are worth as much as the package, the suspicion of bundling falls away.
If they are mere window dressing, it stays.
To find out, the authority is asking those who buy the supplies and those who compete with Google on the market.
This track does not start from scratch.
On April 9, 2025 the authority made the commitments offered by Google binding and closed, with two decisions, the proceedings on Google Automotive Services and Google Maps Platform.

Google had pledged to license the services in the package (Maps, Play and Assistant) as standalone versions too, to drop the clauses that pushed customers toward its own services (such as default settings and the share of advertising revenue) and to create the conditions for interoperability with third-party services.
For the Maps Platform the company had removed the contractual restrictions on combined use with the maps of rivals such as HERE, Mapbox and TomTom.
Google's map content can also appear on third-party maps, such as those of OpenStreetMap.
The effect of those commitments, the Kartellamt specified, did not stop at Germany.

They applied to the infotainment systems of cars that are or could be registered in Germany, and since registration conditions are uniform across the European Union they de facto covered the entire European market.
For the Maps Platform, a billing address in the European Economic Area was enough.
Today's proceeding is meant to clarify whether, beyond the conduct already eliminated, there are further specific restrictions on mapping services for cars.
For drivers nothing changes today, and for quite a while probably not tomorrow either.
This is about contracts between Google and carmakers, not apps to update.
The benefit, if it comes, comes down the chain.
More freedom to combine services means a manufacturer could hand traffic to one supplier and place search to another.
The driver would notice it in fresher maps or a cheaper system, certainly not in a different logo on the screen.
The connected-car market, for that matter, is already crowded with alternative routes.
A manufacturer chooses each time between a system of its own, the Google built into the car and the phone that projects apps onto the screen.
General Motors, for one, put CarPlay back on its pickups after taking it out.
